title: How a mutual fund works
summary: A fund pools money and owns a portfolio of securities on behalf of its unit holders.
body: When you invest, you receive units at the applicable NAV. Your return depends on how the securities and other assets held by the scheme change in value, after scheme expenses. A mutual fund is not a deposit and does not promise a return.

title: What NAV tells you
summary: NAV is the per-unit value of a scheme, calculated from its assets and liabilities.
body: NAV is calculated after valuing the scheme's holdings and accounting for liabilities, then dividing by the units outstanding. A lower NAV does not mean a fund is cheaper or more attractive; compare performance over matching dates and plans instead.

title: Risk comes with returns
summary: Mutual fund values can rise or fall, and past performance cannot assure future results.
body: Market prices, interest rates, credit quality and liquidity can affect scheme NAVs. A fund may lose value, including principal. Consider the scheme's riskometer, investment horizon and your ability to handle losses before investing.

title: Understand fund expenses
summary: Scheme expenses are charged to the fund and reflected in its NAV.
body: Operating and management expenses are charged as a percentage of scheme assets. Direct and regular plans of a scheme have separate expense structures and NAVs. Check the current official disclosure and make sure quoted expense figures use the same definition before comparing funds.

title: Direct and regular plans
summary: The key difference is how the investment is distributed and the associated expense structure.
body: A direct plan is purchased without a distributor and has a separate NAV and expense structure from the regular plan. A regular plan can include distributor services. Choose based on the support you need and compare the costs disclosed for the same plan type.

title: Read the Riskometer
summary: The Riskometer gives a standardized view of a mutual fund scheme's risk level.
body: Use the Riskometer as one input when assessing whether a scheme's risk suits your circumstances. It does not predict returns or remove the possibility of loss. Read the scheme information and reassess when its portfolio or your needs change.
